title: Ego is not you
hookLine: haumai is a veil, not the self; the Gurus never ask for self-hatred

cards: A bathroom mirror after a hot shower, fogged over. Nobody looks at the gray blur and says, well, I suppose I'm fog now. You wipe once, and there you are.
The face was there the whole time; the fog was only on the glass. Yesterday's map leaves a question: what keeps a person from climbing? The Granth's answer has a name, haumai, ego.
And the Gurus talk about it more like fog on a mirror than a stain on a soul.

teach.b: Haumai is the Granth's word for ego: the voice that says I, me, mine, and puts itself at the center of every room. In year one you met it as the disease with its own cure; today asks what it isn't.
In the first stanza of the Japji comes a question. In paraphrase: how does a person become true, and how is the wall of falsehood torn down? Guru Nanak's answer: walk in the hukam, the divine order.

teach.h: A WALL THAT CAN COME DOWN.
teach.b: Haumai is a wall between a person and the One, and a wall can come down. Nobody says the wall is the house. What's underneath?

In Sohila, in the line we met in his aarti, Guru Nanak says that in everyone there is a light, and that light is the One's. So when the fog clears, what's waiting is not something rotten. It is light.

teach.h: AN ILLNESS WITH ITS CURE INSIDE.
teach.b: And in Asa di Var, a salok of Guru Angad calls haumai a long and deep illness, then says the medicine is within it too: by grace, a person lives the Guru's Word. Nobody hates a friend for having a fever.

You bring soup, call the doctor, wait with them. The Granth treats ego as something to heal, and the healing is remembering, not punishing. So a Sikh who catches their own pride isn't asked to despise themselves.
Self-hatred, if you listen closely, can be haumai wearing a sadder coat: still I, still me, still the center of the room. Not self-hatred.

how: Sikhs describe haumai, ego, as the wall or illness that separates a person from the One, and look to the Guru's Word and remembrance of the Name to heal it, rather than to self-punishment.

games.q: what does “ego is not you” mean?
o: haumai is a fog over the light, not the person
a stain on the soul that can never wash out
your true self, which must be fed and protected

games.q: ego in the Granth: tap the pairs.
p: I, me, mine at the center
an illness with its cure inside

s: the Granth treats ego as a person's true self
it calls haumai a wall and an illness; underneath is the One's light.
a salok in Asa di Var says the cure for ego lies within it too
by grace, a person lives the Guru's Word.
despising yourself is the way the Granth offers to beat ego
the cure it names is the Guru's Word; self-hatred can be haumai in a sadder coat.

games.q: you catch yourself being proud and unkind. by the picture in today's lesson, what comes next?
o: decide you are a bad person and stay down on yourself.
treat it like an illness: notice it, and turn to the cure.
ignore it; everyone has an ego.
games.why: Guru Angad's salok calls haumai a long illness whose medicine is within it: by grace, living the Guru's Word.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you did lately that you're not proud of, and notice the voice that shows up to talk about it: is it fair, is it loud?
Set it down, and speak to yourself the way you'd speak to a friend with a fever: that happened, you can make it right, you are more than this. If you pray, let Waheguru come gently on each breath.

wordCard.voice: Ego is not you. Haumai is a wall, a fog, an illness over the light, never the light itself. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: haumai, ego, the I at the center.

carryVoice: Your line: not self-hatred. If the voice against yourself ever turns to thoughts of harming yourself, please reach out now: call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number. Go gently.

sources.ref: Ang 466 (Asa di Var, salok of Guru Angad)
